# Yamaha Vstar 250 won't start: need to diagnose and fix possible fuel, battery, or flooded carb

A sudden inability to crank an engine usually signals one of three culprits: a depleted power source, a blocked airflow path, or a combustion chamber that is too wet to ignite. When a used Yamaha VStar 250 suddenly refuses to turn over after a period of inactivity and high-RPM error handling, the diagnostic process must follow a strict hierarchy of elimination.

The most immediate failure point is almost always the electrical system. You mentioned the battery has not been replaced, even though it was on a tender. Tenders extend battery life by keeping the voltage above critical thresholds, but they do not replenish capacity or repair sulfation caused by deep discharge cycles. If the engine previously exhibited a turning noise followed by a faint buzzing sound, that is the distinct acoustic signature of an alternator struggling against a dead cell structure. The buzzing indicates the starter motor is receiving enough voltage to engage the pinion gear but insufficient current to overcome the mechanical resistance of the flywheel.

In this scenario, the solution is not simply to "jump start" the bike and hope for the best. You must measure the resting voltage at the terminals with a multimeter. A reading below 12.4V indicates a weak battery that cannot sustain the high-amperage draw required by the starter solenoid. Even if the bike starts on reserve, this is a temporary fix that masks the underlying chemical failure. The trade-off here is convenience versus long-term reliability; riding with a marginal battery risks being stranded before you reach your destination, as the alternator may not have enough time to recharge the bank during normal operation.

Once electrical integrity is confirmed or restored via replacement, the next layer of investigation involves the carburetor and fuel mixture. Your description of switching gears up while attempting to start the engine in fifth gear suggests a specific mechanical trauma: severe flooding. By engaging the kickstarter or electric starter while the bike was under load (in gear), you likely spun the flywheel against the compression stroke repeatedly without combustion occurring. This action can force excess fuel into the cylinder, washing away oil from the cylinder walls and creating a mixture that is too rich to ignite.

To diagnose this, remove the air filter cover and inspect the carburetor throat. If the internal passages are coated in black, sticky varnish or if there is liquid pooling in the intake manifold, the carburetor has been flooded. The presence of gas sloshing sounds confirms the fuel level is high, but it does not confirm solvency; old fuel can degrade into gums that clog jets even if it hasn't sat for six months. Attempting to start on reserve is generally ineffective because the reserve float valve often feeds from the same main jet circuit or a poorly regulated overflow line, meaning you are still drawing from contaminated fuel in the primary tank.

The corrective action involves clearing the excess fuel. With the bike on its center stand and the ignition off, remove the fuel cap to allow pressure to equalize, then carefully tilt the motorcycle to drain the carburetor bowls into a waste container. If the engine remains dead after draining, introduce small amounts of fresh fuel directly into the carburetor throat while cranking in neutral with the choke engaged. This bypasses the potentially clogged jets and attempts to ignite the mixture manually.

If the engine still exhibits a buzzing noise but no turning motion after replacing the battery and clearing the carbs, the issue shifts back to the electrical path: check the starter relay and solenoid connections for corrosion or loose terminals that prevent high-current flow. Addressing these layers systematically prevents unnecessary disassembly of the clutch mechanism or timing chain.
